analysis.one_liner: Puts tobacco under FDA authority, imposes billions in fees on manufacturers, bans broadcast tobacco ads, and funds anti-smoking programs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 110 cosponsors, including the House Minority Leader, but died in committee in 1998 without ever getting a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given the FDA legal authority over tobacco products for the first time, locked in the 1996 rules restricting cigarette marketing to children, and imposed a $10 billion initial payment plus rising annual fees (50 cents per pack-equivalent unit in 1999, growing to $1.50) on every tobacco manufacturer. It would have banned tobacco advertising on broadcast and electronic media, required smoke-free public buildings nationwide, set mandatory targets for cutting youth smoking with escalating penalties for manufacturers that missed them, and created an independent board to force the public release of tobacco industry documents. Most of the money would have funded anti-smoking campaigns, quit-smoking programs, research, and payments to states.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, who are the main target of the marketing restrictions, price increases, and reduction targets; non-smokers who would get smoke-free public buildings; current smokers who would get federally funded quit programs; and state governments, which could elect to receive settlement-style payments for tobacco-related health care costs.

how_it_helps.text: Every tobacco manufacturer would owe an immediate $10 billion payment (allocated by market share) plus annual payments of $0.50 per unit in 1999, $1.00 in 2000, and $1.50 thereafter, adjusted for inflation, with most proceeds funding prevention and state grants [S2][S3].

The FDA's 1996 rules on tobacco would be written into law, and new regulations would restrict marketing, advertising, and youth access, require stronger rotating warning labels, and ban tobacco advertising on any broadcast or electronic medium regulated by the FCC [S2][S3].

Manufacturers would face mandatory youth-smoking reduction targets — 33% by years three and four, 50% by five and six, and 80% by year ten — with required price increases, carton-only sales, and plain black-and-white packaging for companies that repeatedly miss the targets [S3].
Public buildings would have to go smoke-free, enforceable by any aggrieved person or government agency, with courts able to award attorney fees and civil penalties up to $5,000 per day [S3].

An independent Tobacco Accountability Board would collect and publish industry documents on health effects, nicotine manipulation, and marketing to children, and investigate company efforts to mislead the public and to influence tobacco laws [S2][S3].

States could elect annual payments equal to what they would have received under the 1997 attorneys-general settlement, and Medicaid would reimburse states for 90% of approved quit-smoking program costs [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers would bear the payments and regulatory costs directly, but they would pass them on to consumers through higher cigarette prices — a cost that falls hardest on low-income adult smokers, which is partly the point of a price-based deterrent. Broadcast media would lose tobacco advertising revenue.

drawbacks.text: The fees and required price increases would make cigarettes more expensive for adult smokers, including low-income smokers who are addicted, a regressive cost that supporters accepted as a deliberate deterrent [S2][S3].
States that elect the federal payments would give up the right to sue manufacturers to recover past tobacco-related health care costs, trading litigation for a fixed payment stream [S3].
Where the bill requires federal warning labels, states and cities could not require additional or different health warnings on packages or in ads, overriding stricter local rules [S3].

The bill largely encoded restrictions from a 1997 proposed resolution negotiated between manufacturers and state attorneys general, so its shape reflected a deal brokered with the industry rather than an independently designed statute [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health gains — fewer children smoking, FDA oversight, public documents, smoke-free buildings, funded cessation — are large and long-lasting, and the main cost falls on the tobacco companies and on smokers through higher prices, which the bill treats as a feature. The genuine weaknesses are the cap on state litigation and the preemption of stronger state warning rules, and the fact that, because the bill built on a settlement framework negotiated with the manufacturers, it stopped short of the strongest regulatory designs public health advocates wanted.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and then to their subcommittees, but no committee ever voted on it and the House adjourned in January 1999 without the bill ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. James V. Hansen (R-UT) introduced the bill on May 14, 1998, with 110 cosponsors — 100 Democrats and 10 Republicans [S1][S4][S5].

The bill was referred the same day to the House Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and on May 26, 1998 it was sent to the Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection and the Health and Environment subcommittees [S5].
No committee action, markup, or floor vote followed; the last recorded action is the May 26 subcommittee referral, and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: they avoided billions in new payments, FDA jurisdiction over their products, advertising bans, mandatory youth-reduction penalties, and the public release of their internal documents. Adult smokers also avoided price increases, and broadcasters kept tobacco ad revenue.

for.name: Rep. James V. Hansen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on May 14, 1998 and recruited a large bipartisan cosponsor list.

for.name: Rep. Richard Gephardt
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Rep. Marty Meehan
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor; he was a leading House author of comprehensive tobacco legislation that year.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: U.S. Representative (CA-29), senior Democrat on the Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor.

against.name: Rep. Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill, leaving it in his committee until Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Newt Gingrich
against.what_they_did: Kept comprehensive tobacco legislation off the House floor in 1998, saying publicly the House would not vote on a tobacco bill that year.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.role: Philip Morris, R.J. Reynolds, Brown & Williamson, Lorillard and allied groups
against.what_they_did: Ran a large-scale lobbying and advertising campaign against comprehensive tobacco regulation in 1997-1998.

sides.party_line_note: The cosponsor list was 100 Democrats and 10 Republicans, so support was heavily Democratic even though the lead sponsor was a Republican; the bill died in committees controlled by Republicans, and no vote was ever taken to test party positions.

industries.note: The bill imposes a $10 billion initial assessment, rising annual per-unit fees, mandatory youth-reduction penalties, advertising bans, FDA jurisdiction, and forced disclosure of internal documents. The companies' revenue depends on continued sales, including to underage smokers targeted by marketing, so their interest ran directly against the bill's public health purpose.

industries.industry: Broadcast and electronic media and tobacco advertisers
industries.note: Advertising tobacco on any medium under FCC jurisdiction would be unlawful, eliminating a large advertising revenue stream. Media profits from the ads depend on the products being sold.

The bill requires state retail licensing, regular compliance inspections, and lets federal authorities suspend retailers' right to sell; brands that repeatedly miss youth-reduction targets could be sold only by the carton. Retail revenue depends on unrestricted sales.

industries.industry: Public health, research, and community clinics
industries.note: The bill funds a $500 million national anti-smoking campaign, $200 million a year for cessation programs through health centers, $1 billion a year for research and surveillance, and 90% Medicaid reimbursement for quit-smoking services. Its interest runs alongside the public's.
